note: HL05 chapter capability ledger. Authored intent, not a derived cache: no validator may rewrite this file. Chapter 1 is deliberately absent — all four of its lessons are still schema v1 with no declared knowledge atoms, so any payoff written for it would be invented rather than derived. That absence is real, measurable debt and must not be papered over with a placeholder.

chapters.title: Give your name
chapters.label: ch:urdu-name
chapters.canDo: I can say my name in Urdu in one sentence, keeping hai at the end where Urdu puts it.

payoff.summary: One sentence with a slot for your own name: merā nām ... hai, with the copula held to the end of the line.

chapters.title: Ask and Answer Names
chapters.label: ch:ur-ask-and-answer-names
chapters.canDo: I can ask someone's name with respectful āp, answer with my own, and close the introduction politely.

payoff.summary: A six-line first meeting: greet, ask āp kā nām kyā hai?, answer with your own name, and close with āp se mil kar khushī huī.

chapters.title: How Are You?
chapters.label: ch:ur-how-are-you
chapters.canDo: I can ask how someone is with respectful āp, choose kaise or kaisī for the person I am addressing, and reply that I am fine, thank you.

payoff.summary: The wellbeing exchange run both ways — āp kaise haiṅ? and āp kaisī haiṅ? — answered with the unchanging maiṅ ṭhīk hūṅ, shukriyā.

chapters.title: Take Leave
chapters.label: ch:ur-take-leave
chapters.canDo: I can open a short Urdu conversation, ask how the other person is, and close it with khudā hāfiz.

payoff.summary: A four-line interaction with a beginning and an end: salām, the wellbeing check, then khudā hāfiz from both voices.

chapters.title: Five Verbs at the Core
chapters.label: ch:ur-core-verbs
chapters.canDo: I can name five everyday Urdu verbs by their shared -nā ending, take that ending off to reach the stem, and say what I do in the present with the participle agreeing for gender and the copula agreeing for person.

payoff.summary: The fifth verb runs the whole machine at once: strip -nā from all five infinitives, hold the doubled nūn that keeps jānnā apart from jānā, and put the stem into maiṅ jāntā/jāntī hūṅ.

chapters.title: Four Verbs of the Mind
chapters.label: ch:ur-mind-verbs
chapters.canDo: I can say that I think, understand, read and write in Urdu, take the -nā off each verb to reach its stem, and read the two-eyed he that turns a plain consonant into an aspirated one.

payoff.summary: The fourth verb arrives with no new letters at all: read لکھنا straight off, then run all four stems through maiṅ ...tā/tī hūṅ and sort the chapter's inherited verbs from the borrowed words for pen, book and script.

chapters.title: Four Verbs Between People
chapters.label: ch:ur-social-verbs
chapters.canDo: I can take, ask and help in Urdu, build a verb by bolting a borrowed noun onto karnā, and say what I like in the sentence where the thing liked is the subject and I am only the person it happens to.

payoff.summary: mujhe paṛhnā pasand hai — the first Urdu sentence the learner cannot open with maiṅ. It closes over the chapter's own four verbs by dropping each -nā infinitive into the liked-thing slot, and reuses madad karnā's join in pasand karnā.

chapters.title: People You'd Introduce
chapters.label: ch:ur-people
chapters.canDo: I can name my brother, sister, friend and family in Urdu, and choose merā or merī correctly for each noun's grammatical gender.

payoff.summary: Say merā bhāī, merī bahan, merā dost and merā khāndān with merā/merī chosen correctly for each noun, and sort the four into inherited bhāī/bahan against Persian dost/khāndān — the same native-versus-borrowed split Chapter 8's verbs drew.

chapters.title: Four Words on the Face
chapters.label: ch:ur-face-words
chapters.canDo: I can name my ear, nose, eye and mouth in Urdu, notice that kān and nāk share the same three letters reversed, and read the nūn that marks a nasal vowel instead of a spoken consonant.

payoff.summary: Name kān, nāk, āṅkh and muṅh, explain the plain nūn that nasalizes āṅkh and muṅh against the dedicated ں of maiṅ and hūṅ, and count three settled Indo-European cousins found this chapter — nāk/nose, āṅkh/eye — against kān's honest dead end.

chapters.title: The Heart
chapters.label: ch:ur-heart
chapters.canDo: I can name my heart in Urdu and trace dil to the same Indo-European root as Sanskrit hṛdaya and English heart, arriving by the Persian road instead of the Sanskrit one.

payoff.summary: Say merā dil, and trace it through Middle Persian and Proto-Iranian back to the same PIE *ḱērd- that gives Sanskrit hṛdaya, English heart, Latin cor and Greek kardía — dil and hṛdaya split at the Indo-Iranian fork, not opposite lineages but the same root by two roads, echoing pūchhnā and porsīdan.

chapters.title: Water, Tea, Milk, Bread
chapters.label: ch:ur-food-words
chapters.canDo: I can name water, tea, milk and bread in Urdu, say what I like using the frame Chapter 8 built, and sort each word as inherited or Persian.

payoff.summary: Say mujhe roṭī pasand hai, reusing Chapter 8's dative-experiencer frame on a plain noun instead of an infinitive, and sort pānī/dūdh/roṭī as inherited against chāy's Persian loan — with pānī reusing lenā's verb frame and dūdh correcting a tempting false cognate with English dough.
